vignette:
Adaeze Okonkwo is a 42-year-old Nigerian-American woman who works as a train conductor for a regional rail service in the mid-Atlantic United States. She has been married for eleven years and presents for psychological treatment following what she describes as nearly two years of symptoms she can no longer manage on her own.

Approximately twenty-six months ago, while visiting extended family in a West African country experiencing significant civil unrest, Adaeze was detained by a paramilitary faction at an informal checkpoint. What followed over the next several days involved systematic physical abuse carried out in a concrete holding room. Her captors used burning implements during some of the sessions, and the smell of scorched material - cloth, skin - became inseparable from the experience of helplessness and pain. At various points the room fell into complete, deliberate silence before a guard entered, a silence that preceded the worst of what was done to her. She witnessed injuries on the bodies of other detainees held in the same space - lacerations, burns - and these images lodged themselves in her memory with a clarity that has not faded. She was eventually released through the intervention of a family contact and returned to the United States, where she disclosed only the barest outline of what had occurred to her husband before withdrawing into silence about it entirely.

In the months following her return, Adaeze found herself unable to construct a coherent account of what had happened, even privately. When she tries to recall the detention, what surfaces are not sequential events but fragments - a visual flash of a wound on a man's forearm, the particular quality of light in the room, a posture. She has described these images as arriving without warning and without context, and when they do, she has said that she does not feel she is remembering something past but that she is, in some immediate and bodily sense, back inside it. She cannot narrate the experience as a story with a beginning and an end, and this has left her with the unsettling sense that it has never truly concluded.

Her working life has become a site of considerable distress. As a conductor, Adaeze moves through carriages where passengers shift and reach for luggage and turn suddenly in their seats. Each abrupt movement in her peripheral vision pulls her body into an immediate state of alarm that she cannot talk herself out of, even when she recognises the person is simply standing to exit. She has developed the habit of scanning the length of each car before she walks it, and she has become attuned to the sounds of the train in a way that her colleagues have noticed - she pauses, head tilted, when the ambient noise changes. What she is listening for, she knows, is the specific quality of sudden silence, the kind that in her memory meant someone was about to come through a door. On the platform and in her home alike, she finds herself unable to let her body settle. She had come to believe that relaxation itself was a form of exposure, that lowering her vigilance for even a short time was the condition under which something terrible became possible again.

At home she has begun scanning for sounds near the entry points of the house each night before bed, and she has taken to rehearsing in careful mental detail what she would do if various worst-case situations unfolded - not because this brings her peace, but because she is certain that being unprepared is more dangerous than the anxiety the rehearsal costs her. She checks her arms and torso regularly, running her hands over her skin in a way she finds difficult to explain to herself. She began smoking cigarettes within weeks of returning home, which she recognises as incongruous given how profoundly the smell of smoke disturbs her in other contexts, and she has not been able to stop.

Her husband has grown distant in his worry, uncertain how to reach her. She has said little to him about the content of what she experiences. What finally brought Adaeze to seek help was a shift last month during which she froze on a platform after a passenger with a bandaged hand walked past her. She stood motionless for nearly a minute before a colleague intervened. She is afraid, above all, that she will not be able to keep her job. What she hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to tell someone - perhaps eventually herself - what actually happened.
